anchorData: KNIFE PHENOMENON: Mama Wanjiru pushes with the same hand force of 40 N on both knives. Both knives cut a length of 5 cm (0.05 m) of contact. Sharp knife: edge thickness 0.1 mm = 0.0001 m, contact area = 0.05 x 0.0001 = 0.000005 m2 (5 x 10^-6 m2), pressure = 40 / 0.000005 = 8,000,000 Pa = 8 MPa. Blunt knife: edge thickness 1 mm = 0.001 m, contact area = 0.05 x 0.001 = 0.00005 m2 (5 x 10^-5 m2), pressure = 40 / 0.00005 = 800,000 Pa = 0.8 MPa. The sharp edge has 10 times less area and gives 10 times more pressure (8 MPa vs 0.8 MPa). Model value: a tomato skin or nyama choma surface gives way at about 2 MPa. So sharp (8 MPa) is greater than 2 MPa and cuts; blunt (0.8 MPa) is less than 2 MPa and only squashes. BRICK ON SAND/FLOUR (L2-3): brick mass 2 kg, weight = 2 x 10 = 20 N. Faces: large 20 cm x 10 cm = 200 cm2 = 0.02 m2, pressure 20/0.02 = 1,000 Pa; medium 20 cm x 5 cm = 100 cm2 = 0.01 m2, pressure 20/0.01 = 2,000 Pa; small 10 cm x 5 cm = 50 cm2 = 0.005 m2, pressure 20/0.005 = 4,000 Pa. Same weight, the smallest face sinks deepest. CAMEL vs PERSON (L3): camel mass 400 kg, weight 4,000 N, four feet of 0.05 m2 each = 0.2 m2 total, pressure = 4,000/0.2 = 20,000 Pa = 20 kPa. Same camel weight on narrow hooves of total 0.04 m2 would give 4,000/0.04 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. Person mass 60 kg, weight 600 N, two shoes total 0.04 m2, pressure = 600/0.04 = 15,000 Pa = 15 kPa. The camel is about 6.7 times heavier (4,000/600) but its pressure on sand (20 kPa) is only a little larger than the person's (15 kPa). CAN WITH HOLES (L4-5): holes at depths 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm (0.05, 0.10, 0.15 m). Water (density 1,000 kg/m3) pressure: 500 Pa, 1,000 Pa, 1,500 Pa. At 10 cm (0.10 m): water 1,000 Pa, salt water (1,030 kg/m3) 1,030 Pa, cooking oil (920 kg/m3) 920 Pa. Lower holes squirt farther. DAM AND LAKE (L4, L6, L9): dam water depth 30 m, pressure at base = 1,000 x 10 x 30 = 300,000 Pa = 300 kPa; at 10 m depth = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa. Lake Victoria point at depth 40 m: pressure from water alone = 1,000 x 10 x 40 = 400,000 Pa = 400 kPa. At 10 m: 100 kPa. At 20 m: 200 kPa. ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE (L7): approx Mombasa (sea level) 101 kPa = 101,000 Pa; Kisumu (about 1,130 m) 89 kPa; Nairobi (about 1,800 m) 83 kPa; Mount Kenya summit (5,199 m) about 54 kPa. Glass with cardboard: mouth area 40 cm2 = 0.004 m2, upward force of air = 101,000 x 0.004 = 404 N; water weight (250 g) = 2.5 N, so the cardboard stays. HYDRAULIC JACK (L8-9): small piston 5 cm2 = 0.0005 m2, large piston 100 cm2 = 0.01 m2 (20 times bigger); effort 50 N on small piston gives pressure 50/0.0005 = 100,000 Pa = 100 kPa; load force on large piston = 100,000 x 0.01 = 1,000 N (20 times 50 N). Small piston moves 20 times farther than the large piston.
characters: Mama Wanjiru: cook in a kitchen in Kisumu preparing sukuma wiki, tomatoes and nyama choma; always pushes with 40 N. Sharp knife: edge 0.1 mm thick, keeps its edge. Blunt knife: same size and shape, edge 1 mm thick. Brick: 2 kg, 20 cm x 10 cm x 5 cm, used on a tray of flour or sand. Camel: 400 kg, wide soft feet, walks on desert sand in northern Kenya (Turkana, Marsabit). Person: 60 kg student in school shoes. Can with three holes: tin or plastic bottle with holes at 5, 10, 15 cm filled with water. Lake Victoria (Kisumu, Kenya): used for depth-pressure examples with fresh water of density 1,000 kg/m3. Dam: a Kenyan dam (e.g. Masinga) used as a generic dam with water 30 m deep; the wall is built thicker at the bottom. Mama Wanjiru's family garage mechanic (Mzee Otieno) uses a hydraulic jack to lift a matatu, effort 50 N lifts 1,000 N. Nairobi, Kisumu, Mombasa and Mount Kenya: places for atmospheric pressure values.
outcome: The force from Mama Wanjiru's hand is the same (40 N) for both knives, but the sharp knife's thin edge touches the food over a much smaller area (5 x 10^-6 m2 compared with 5 x 10^-5 m2), so the pressure is 10 times greater (8 MPa compared with 0.8 MPa). The sharp knife's pressure is above what a tomato or meat can withstand (about 2 MPa), so it cuts, while the blunt knife's pressure is below it, so the food is only squashed. So the difference between the knives is the area, not the force, and pressure = force / area explains the phenomenon.
conventions: Pressure is force acting normally (at right angles) per unit area on a surface: P = F / A. Use the name 'pressure' (not 'stress'). Units: pressure in pascals (Pa), 1 Pa = 1 N/m2; 1 kPa = 1,000 Pa; 1 MPa = 1,000,000 Pa. Force and weight in newtons (N); area in m2 (1 m2 = 10,000 cm2; 1 cm2 = 0.0001 m2). Weight W = mg, with g = 10 N/kg (always use 10, not 9.8). Mass in kg; density rho in kg/m3 (water 1,000; salt water 1,030; cooking oil 920). Depth h in metres measured vertically from the liquid surface. Liquid pressure formula: P = rho g h (pressure due to the liquid only, called liquid pressure). Atmospheric pressure is written P_atm, approximately 101 kPa at sea level. Total pressure under a liquid = P_atm + rho g h, only when the lesson states it. Fluid means liquid or gas. Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Hydraulic relation: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2. Symbols: F, A, P, m, g, rho, h. Always give a number with its unit. Always state 'same force, different area' when explaining the knives. Use Kenyan examples only.

lessonMap.focus: Anchoring phenomenon: sharp vs blunt knife
lessonMap.teaches: Launching the question: students observe that the same force gives different cutting results and record initial ideas, the DQB and an initial model (no formula yet).
lessonMap.buildsOn: No earlier lesson; students' everyday experience of cutting food.
lessonMap.usesData: KNIFE PHENOMENON: 40 N for both knives, sharp edge 0.1 mm and blunt edge 1 mm (observations only, no pressure calculation).

lessonMap.teaches: Pressure depends on both force and area, defined as P = F/A with unit pascal (Pa).
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: the DQB question about what differs between the knives, and the idea that force is the same.
lessonMap.usesData: BRICK ON SAND/FLOUR: weight 20 N, three faces and pressures 1,000 / 2,000 / 4,000 Pa.

lessonMap.teaches: Using P = F/A to calculate and compare pressures when area changes, and applying it to explain how the sharp knife works (inverse relationship between area and pressure for a constant force).
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: P = F/A and the brick results; Lesson 1: the knife observations and initial model.
lessonMap.usesData: KNIFE PHENOMENON calculations (8 MPa vs 0.8 MPa) and CAMEL vs PERSON (20 kPa, 100 kPa on hooves, 15 kPa).

lessonMap.teaches: Liquids exert pressure that increases with depth, shown by the can with holes, and why dam walls are thicker at the bottom.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2-3: pressure as force per area on a surface (now applied to liquids).
lessonMap.usesData: CAN WITH HOLES at 5, 10, 15 cm (500, 1,000, 1,500 Pa for water, qualitative first) and DAM 30 m (300 kPa).

lessonMap.teaches: Liquid pressure depends on depth and density (not on container shape or amount of liquid), and acts equally in all directions at the same depth.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 4: pressure increases with depth, the can with holes.
lessonMap.usesData: WATER vs SALT WATER vs OIL at 10 cm: 1,000 / 1,030 / 920 Pa with densities 1,000 / 1,030 / 920 kg/m3.

lessonMap.teaches: Deriving P = rho g h from P = F/A (weight of a liquid column) and using it to calculate liquid pressure at given depths.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2 and 5: P = F/A, W = mg, depth and density as factors.
lessonMap.usesData: LAKE VICTORIA: 10 m = 100 kPa, 20 m = 200 kPa, 40 m = 400 kPa; DAM 30 m = 300 kPa.

lessonMap.teaches: Air has weight and so exerts atmospheric pressure (about 101 kPa at sea level) that decreases with altitude, with effects such as the inverted glass, crushed can, ears popping and drinking straw.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2 and 6: P = F/A and pressure from the weight of a column of fluid (the atmosphere as a column of air).
lessonMap.usesData: ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE: Mombasa 101 kPa, Kisumu 89 kPa, Nairobi 83 kPa, Mount Kenya 54 kPa; glass mouth 0.004 m2, force 404 N vs water 2.5 N.

lessonMap.focus: Transmission of pressure in fluids (Pascal's principle)
lessonMap.teaches: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions, so a small force on a small piston gives a larger force on a larger piston (F1/A1 = F2/A2), in syringes, hydraulic jacks and brakes.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2-3: P = F/A and area effect; Lesson 5: pressure acts in all directions in liquids.
lessonMap.usesData: HYDRAULIC JACK: 5 cm2 and 100 cm2 pistons, 50 N effort, 100 kPa, 1,000 N load.

lessonMap.teaches: Synthesis, with no new formula: using the siphon (pressure difference with atmospheric pressure and depth), dams and hydraulic devices as applications, finalising the class model and revisiting the DQB to fully explain the knife phenomenon.
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1-8, especially Lesson 3 (area and pressure for the knives), Lessons 6-7 (liquid and atmospheric pressure) and Lesson 8 (hydraulics).
lessonMap.usesData: KNIFE PHENOMENON (8 MPa vs 0.8 MPa vs 2 MPa threshold), DAM 30 m, HYDRAULIC JACK 50 N to 1,000 N, and ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURE 101 kPa.
